title: Safety/Tolerability/Immunogenicity of first-in-human Aβ DNA vaccine, AV-1959D Phase 1 trials in early-stage AD subjects: based on IND18953 cleared by FDA.
text:
The first-in-human DNA vaccine, AV-1959D based on MultiTEP platform is designed (i) to
augment anti-Aβ antibody production without activation of potentially harmful autoreactive Th cells
(ii) to activate Th cells specific to foreign epitopes incorporated in MultiTEP, providing broad
coverage of the targeted population with high MHC class II gene polymorphism and (iii) to activate
naïve and memory Th cells overcoming the immunosenescence in the older people. Of note,
due to an ethical imperative raised by the FDA during our pre-IND meeting, we propose Phase 1
safety/tolerability/immunogenicity trials of AV-1959D in early stage AD patients based on
IND18953 cleared by the FDA in April 2020 prior to initiating the preventive trials in asymptomatic
people at risk of MCI/AD.

title: Hematologic Malignancies
text: Blood cancers afflict children and adults and are life-threatening. The Hematologic Malignancies (HM) Program is dedicated to understanding the causes of blood cancers and developing successful gene, drug, and cellular treatment options to improve the quality of life and survival of patients. These goals are accomplished through four major aims: 1) create a deeper understanding of the biologic basis of hematological malignancies; 2) enhance our knowledge of hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) biology and our capabilities for gene therapy of hematological malignancies; 3) develop novel non-transplant treatments; and 4) improve the availability, safety, and efficacy of hematopoietic cell transplantation. These complementary and intersecting aims bring together multidisciplinary expertise in hematology, immunology, genomics, clinical trial design/implementation, computation, and biostatistics. Synergy across the research aims is achieved through close collaborations with patients and providers, interactions with COE, CRTEC, and PED, and a well-integrated network of clinical and research faculty. The HM Program currently has 105 members from all three Consortium institutions. Broad expertise of clinicians and clinical and basic scientists provide a deep skill set to successfully accomplish the program’s aims. The scientific goals are supported by the complementary expertise of Program Co-Leaders Dr. Fred Appelbaum (non-transplant) and Dr. Effie Petersdorf (transplant) and by Associate Program Leaders Dr. Janis Abkowitz (leukemia biology) and Dr. Hans-Peter Kiem (gene therapy). The structural organization of faculty with a disease (adult leukemia; pediatric leukemia; myeloma; myelodysplasia; lymphoma) and research (myeloid stem cell biology; gene therapy; radio-immunotherapy; hematopoietic cell transplantation; long-term follow-up) focus enhances collaborations within and across the program. Program members currently have $38.7M in research funding of which $12.1M is from NCI. Large P01, U19, U54, and U01 grants to the faculty support extensive intra- and interprogrammatic collaborations across the four aims. Program members published 1,655 papers in the previous grant period. 455 were intraprogrammatic and 459 were interprogrammatic. These significant inter- and intraprogrammatic interactions animate extensive cross-theme collaborations.

title: Project 01: Cancer Biology (CB)
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – CANCER BIOLOGY (CB) The Cancer Biology (CB) Program at The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center (OSUCCC), led by Matthew Ringel, MD, Dawn Chandler, PhD, and Gina Sizemore, PhD, has 66 members from 30 academic departments. CB is a fundamental basic science program with a vision to facilitate and drive transformative mechanistic research in cancer biology and progression to improve cancer outcomes through translational collaborations emphasizing the priority cancers in our catchment area (CA). The Specific Aims of the CB Program are: 1) Gene regulation and deregulation in cancer. Studies focus on identifying and mechanistically studying how genes are differentially controlled in cancer biology; 2) Mechanisms of cancer progression. Studies focus on understanding cancer progression and treatment resistance emphasizing the development and use of novel technologies; and 3) Tumor microenvironment and immuno-oncology. Studies focus on fundamental research on tumor microenvironment and tumor-immune interactions that regulate cancer growth and provide therapeutic opportunities. To achieve these aims, CB investigators concentrate on key scientific areas including: 1) defining new regulatory networks and immune-tumor interactions leading to cancer initiation and progression; 2) developing new robust cancer models and using them for reproducible functional identification of pathways regulating primary tumor invasion and brain, bone, and liver metastases; and 3) fundamental studies addressing cellular response to environmental challenges including hypoxia, tissue barriers, infection, and therapies. The CB Program is a cohesive program that promotes and supports collaborative high impact basic science research. In the current cycle, in comparison to the prior funding cycle, CB had a 16% increase in cancer-relevant publications with an emphasis on collaboration as evidenced by an 80% increase in intra-programmatic collaborative publications and a 64% increase in inter-programmatic collaborative publications. In addition, there was a more than doubling (113% increase) of publications in high impact (Impact factor ≥10) journals. Similarly, the CB program overall cancer-related direct funding increased by 75% over the last 5 years including a 23% increase in NCI funding. CB emphasizes career development of its members, supports and promotes community involvement in its research mission, and stresses inter-programmatic collaboration in alignment with the OSUCCC strategic plan. CB supports these goals by holding monthly program meetings, providing pilot funds, providing structured member training and education with Cancer Research Training and Education (CRTEC), offering community interactions with Community Outreach and Engagement (COE), and facilitating engagement with the interprogrammatic themes of the OSUCCC. Future plans include innovation in cancer biology with emphasis on priority CA cancers through development of new technologies, including tissue model systems, RNA- and nano-therapeutics, applications of machine learning/artificial intelligence for multi-omics data sets, assessment of new regulators of the tumor immune environment, and partnerships with clinical/translational scientists to improve prevention and treatment of cancer.

title: Vitamin A metabolism in hair cycle regulation
text:
8. Project Narrative:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it will provide insight into the sex dependent
regulation of vitamin A metabolism in hair follicle stem cell regulation, hair follicle stem cell loss, and hair loss,
which will ultimately lead to more targeted and effective retinoid treatments. Thus, the proposed research is
relevant to the NIAMS mission to understand the pathways that regulate hair follicle stem cells.

title: Delivery of Turtle Island Tales to Promote Family Wellness
text: American Indian (AI) communities experience profound health and economic differences across the lifespan, including increased risk for obesity, cancer, food insecurity (FI), and poverty. Overwhelming evidence indicates obesity prevention evidence-based interventions (EBIs) reduce cancer risk, but the degree to which EBIs have been developed in culturally relevant ways or to reach large numbers of AI families is extremely limited. Community engaged dissemination and implementation (CEDI) strategies are needed across multiple social ecological levels to increase EBI adoption, implementation, and maintenance in AI communities. Our objective is to increase the reach of EBIs for cancer and obesity prevention among AI families who live in persistent poverty areas (PPAs). The proposed project, Delivery of Turtle Island Tales to Promote Family Wellness (Turtle Island Tales), is a participatory action research project designed to improve local capacity for sustained EBI impact. Turtle Island Tales is a family-focused, home-based EBI for childhood obesity prevention named to acknowledge Turtle Island as the term for North America used by many AI communities. Turtle Island Tales will be conducted across four state Cooperative Extension Systems (Extension) in AI communities with ~4,000 children and their families in PPAs in rural and frontier areas. Turtle Island Tales engages system, community, and organizational partners to identify, refine, and develop CEDI strategies to address both disease prevention and FI. A Project Steering Committee and Local Community Advisory Boards will conduct iterative planning and evaluation using outcomes specified in the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance (RE-AIM) framework. For Aim 1, we will facilitate and evaluate the reach of T-Tales in PPAs within AI communities in Montana, Oregon, South Dakota, and Wisconsin when delivered by Extension; determine the effectiveness of T-Tales for health behavior change, and evaluate the reduction in FI among participating families by facilitating connections with community- and system-level resources (e.g., Extension, WIC). For Aim 2, we will evaluate the state-level adoption, implementation, and organizational maintenance capacity of Extension and AI communities for T-Tales and determine budget impacts of implementing T-Tales into sustained Extension delivery. We expect to generate a novel CEDI Strategies Toolkit to move obesity and cancer prevention EBIs into sustained community implementation and account for the unique social and cultural contexts in AI communities in PPAs. Findings will advance the field of CEDI science through the co-production of strategies to influence EBI adoption, implementation, and maintenance using an innovative conceptual framework that leverages social ecological, dissemination and implementation, behavioral, and solution-oriented approach to health disparities frameworks to prevent obesity and cancer in AI families in PPAs.

title: Mechanisms of gene regulation in bacterial defense islands
text:
Bacteria encode diverse immune systems that protect their host from infection by bacteriophages, but whether
and how these systems are regulated at the gene expression level is not well understood. I will
comprehensively identify and define the transcriptional regulators that control bacterial immune systems in
response to phage infection and other environmental stresses including DNA damage. This work will result in a
more complete understanding of how bacteria respond to bacteriophage infections, thereby aiding the
development of effective bacteriophage therapies to address the rise in multidrug-resistant bacterial
pathogens.

title: Passive social media use, coping, and momentary stress in geospatial context: longitudinal effects on mental health and intermediate biological pathways in a sample of White and Black adolescents
text: There is increasing concern that social media use may be impacting mental health in adolescents. The goal of this proposal is to determine if using social media passively is related to mental health as well as characterize physiological pathways (e.g. parasympathetic nervous system) that influence risk for poor mental and physical health. Additionally, we will examine how self-reported stressors and geospatial exposures to stressful environments (i.e. streets with high levels of violent crime) impact frequency of passive social media use and the degree to which passive social media use as stress coping strategy alters emotional and physiological responses to stressors.

title: Comparative Genomics and Data Science Core
text: COMPARATIVE GENOMICS AND DATA SCIENCE (CGDS) CORE PROJECT SUMMARY Computational genomics and bioinformatics are now an essential aspect of nearly all genetic studies of regeneration, while genomic studies are similarly changing how we view aging. With new discoveries of transcriptional dysregulation leading to aging/inflammatory states and epigenetic "clocks" impacting gene expression as we age, all biological disciplines now require bioinformatics expertise to plan experiments, acquire and manage data, interpret findings, and integrate results in public repositories. The Comparative Genomics and Data Science (CGDS) Core (formerly the Comparative Functional Genomics Core) was established in COBRE phases I and II and provided essential support to investigators working in the Kathryn W. Davis Center for Regenerative Biology and Aging. CGDS Core staff members have broad expertise in analyzing genome-scale data sets including transcriptomic, proteomic, epigenetic, non-coding RNA, and genetic variation data. The CGDS Core Director Dr. Graber has over twenty-five years of experience in computational analysis of genome-scale biological data, spanning multiple data types and divergent organisms ranging from yeast to mammals. During COBRE Phases I and II, CGDS Core personnel provided essential services in experimental design, data analysis, and education to all COBRE Project Leaders. The CGDS Core will build upon its successes to establish a self-sustaining bioinformatics and data science core in Phase III. The goals of the CGDS Core are 1) to provide both standard service and collaborative levels of bioinformatic support to core users and collaborators, 2) continue to transition bioinformatic analysis pipelines to cloud computing, 3) to educate and empower our users to perform their own bioinformatic and statistical analyses, 4) Establish evaluation metrics for the core in conjunction with the external advisory committee and 5) enact a user fee schedule to ensure long term sustainability of the CGDS core. The proposed CGDS core incorporates state of the art bioinformatic services with the flexibility to engage with core users at multiple levels of investigation. Continued bioinformatic education of users will empower a new generation of investigators and allow for increased focus on innovation and new analytical pipelines as core services. Consolidation of common data formats and broad access to data and analysis pipelines through cloud computing are the current direction of bioinformatic and biomedical data processing and curation. Implementing these core services will enable experimental innovation and increase research impact for CGDS core users.

title: Leveraging innate immunity for GIST therapy
text:
This project will contribute to the scientific community’s understanding of how the human body’s immune
system helps protect against gastrointestinal stromal tumors, a type of lethal tumor arising from the
connective tissue of the gut. More importantly, however, it will uncover how we can stimulate the immune
response to target these tumors. This has the potential to improve systemic therapy when given in
combination with imatinib, the gold standard drug, as well as open the door to new treatment options for
imatinib-resistant disease.

title: Elucidating the signaling and protein interaction networks of the O-GlcNAc transferase during embryonic stem cell state transitions
text:
O-GlcNAc is the only known intracellular glycosylation signaling pathway in mammals, and is implicated in nearly
every basic biological process from signal transduction and gene expression to cell division and differentiation.
Despite its widespread reach, we lack a foundational understanding of this post-translational modification, largely
due to the lack of tools to unambiguously identify O-GlcNAcylated proteins or to perturb the essential O-GlcNAc
transferase gene (Ogt). Here, we propose to apply new groundbreaking tools we have recently developed to
uncover the principles of O-GlcNAc signaling, including its dynamics, how its propagated, and its role in
transcriptional control of stem cell differentiation.

title: Novel retinal higher-order capillary hemodynamics imaging for detecting cerebral small vessel disease
text: Cerebral small vessel disease is a major cause of stroke, cognitive impairment, and dementia, but early and sensitive tools for detecting microvascular dysfunction remain limited. This project will develop a noninvasive retinal imaging approach to measure capillary blood-flow dynamics that may improve detection, monitoring, and understanding of cerebral small vessel disease. The resulting biomarkers could support earlier intervention and help reduce the public health burden of vascular brain injury and dementia.

title: The role of TREM2 in Alzheimer's disease related neuropathogenesis in people with HIV
text:
Worldwide, over 34 million people are infected with HIV, and as high as 50% of HIV patients are affected by HIV-
associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND), despite the success of antiretroviral therapy (ART). As these
patients live longer with ART, they face increased risk of age-related comorbidities, such as the development of
Alzheimer's Disease. The proposed studies will probe underlying mechanisms of HIV-induced neurotoxicity that
may lead to novel therapeutic interventions for HAND and other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Rational Design of Next-Generation Engineered T Cells for Enhanced Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
T cells engineered to express 4-1BB chimeric antigen receptors (4-1BB CARs) have shown promises for effective
cancer treatment, but the long-term therapeutic efficacy remains challenging. In this study, we propose novel
strategies to harness 4-1BB efficiently in order to improve the efficacy of 4-1BB CARs. Furthermore, we aim to
identify key factors important for potent 4-1BB signaling, which will advance our knowledge for targeting 4-1BB
for improved T cell function.

title: Physiology Core
text: Abstract The Physiology Core provides a series of graded technologies and expertise to investigators who wish to address fundamental questions about transport processes that occur in the tubular structures of the nephron and other relevant systems. To gain understanding of biological processes that mediate kidney function in health and disease states, in light of the phenotypic diversity and functional complexity of this organ, the use of strategies that allow specific nephron segments/cells/proteins to be studied in isolation under defined conditions is required. The Core, through its three Subcores, offers expertise and state-of-the-art technologies for studying the function and regulation of transport and other membrane resident proteins with progressive degrees of complexity from single molecules to model systems to native epithelia. The Single Tubule and Microperfusion Subcore provides tools and technologies to study the function and expression of transport proteins and associated regulatory pathways in single nephron segments isolated from small mammals and kidney organoids. The Electrophysiology Subcore provides expertise and a toolbox of electrophysiological approaches to study the function and regulation of transport proteins at the molecular and cellular levels in model systems and native epithelia. The Live-Cell Imaging Subcore offers imaging tools and technologies to assess ion transport, changes in membrane potential, cellular volume, intracellular mediators, and signaling molecules in immortalized cells and native preparations using chemical and genetically encoded fluorescent sensors. The Core will apply a multipronged approach and collaborate with the O’Brien Consortium to share specialized resources and technologies throughout the kidney research community, to lower the barrier to entry for early-stage investigators and researchers new to the kidney field, and to advance kidney research and discovery nationwide.

title: CT Based Scalable Medical Artificial Intelligence for Recalcitrant Cancers Screening and Early Detection
text:
We will develop AI algorithms to detect very small cancers of the pancreas, hepatobiliary system, and upper
GI tract on indicated CT scans ordered because of symptoms, abnormal lab results, or high-risk status, so
patients can be diagnosed and treated sooner. We will also adapt these tools for the millions of opportunistic
CTs done for other reasons (for example, after injuries), including non-contrast scans, to flag early warning
signs, track changes over time, and recommend indicated follow-up imaging when needed. Finally, we will test
the tools on CT datasets curated from JHU, Stanford, and UCSF, as well as public international collections with
diverse patient demographics and imaging protocols, to show earlier detection, fewer missed cases, and
clearer next steps—creating a scalable safety net that can extend to many cancers beyond these three.

title: Optoelectronics integrated multimodal heart tissue platform for online probing of cardiac physiology and therapeutic screening
text:
The goal of this project is to develop the first “all-in-one” high throughput heart tissue slice culture and analysis
systems that combine the key features of microfluidic tissue culture systems, optical microscopy systems,
transparent multielectrode arrays, circuits, control and data analysis capabilities in a volumetrically efficient form
factor. The platforms will allow for automated, efficient chronic culture of human adult heart tissue slices and
real-time continuous on-chip multiparametric monitoring/control of vital cardiac parameters and their
interconnections at both cellular and tissue levels. This technology will greatly improve the fidelity, simplify the
operation, and expand the possibilities in studying heart disease mechanisms and accurate preclinical drug
screening.

title: Unraveling the Functional Redundancy and Activation Mechanisms of Enterococcal Proteases in Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections (CAUTI)
text:
This research will advance our understanding of how enterococcal proteases GelE and SprE contribute to
the pathogenesis of catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI), elucidating their regulatory
mechanisms, functional roles, and therapeutic potential. By uncovering these proteases' contributions to biofilm
stability and tissue invasion, this work will lay the groundwork for developing antibiotic-sparing treatments to
combat biofilm-associated infections, ultimately enhancing patient outcomes and reducing the burden of
antibiotic resistance.

title: Roles of Autophagy in Microglial Senescence and Parkinsons Disease
text:
The greatest risk factor for developing Parkinson’s disease, outweighing all others, is age. However, it is unclear
how aging predisposes the brain to PD. This project studies the mechanism of how microglia become senescent,
characterizes the senescent microglia, and determines the impact of senescent microglia on dopaminergic
neurons using human Parkinson’s disease postmortem brains and human microglia derived from induced
pluripotent stem cells.

title: Molecular Genetics of Bacteria and Phages Conference
text:
The Molecular Genetics of Bacteria and Phages (MGBP) Meeting provides training, career
development, and networking opportunities for both young and established scientists who seek
to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying the basic physiology of bacteria and phages
and how they interact with each other and their hosts. The focus of the MGBP Meeting is directly
applicable to the scientific missions supported by the National Institutes of Health, including the
support of both basic and applied research to understand, prevent, and treat infectious diseases.

title: CardioPredict ML: Machine Learning-enhanced Cardiovascular Risk Assessment for Preconception Care
text:
This project will allow for risk assessment for cardiovascular complications of pregnancy among women of
reproductive age who wish to become pregnant. It will provide an avenue for women to make informed
decisions regarding their reproductive health and work with their healthcare team to ensure the best possible
outcomes. It will also allow for early intervention with cardio-obstetric care on the side of healthcare
providers, as the majority of pregnancy-related care is given after conception.
